title: The long wait
hookLine: survivors, many of them widows, waited decades for justice, while the years that followed brought violence to many Punjabi families of every background

cards: In west Delhi there's a neighborhood people have long called the Widow Colony.
After November 1984, many women who had lost husbands, sons and brothers in a few days were moved there, into small flats, often with young children. They went to work. They raised their kids.
And year after year, they went to hearings, stood in front of commissions, and told the same story again. Some grew old doing it. Some died before any court said a word.

teach.b: After November 1984 came commission after commission, committee after committee: around ten of them over twenty years. Reports were written. Few people were punished.
In 2005, the Prime Minister, himself a Sikh, apologized in parliament.

teach.h: AN APOLOGY, A VERDICT, DECADES ON.
teach.b: In 2018, more than thirty years later, a court sentenced a senior politician to life in prison for his part. For the widows, some of it came too late, and some has never come. And the long wait wasn't only in Delhi.
In Punjab, the years after 1984 brought a decade of violence that reached families of every background. Armed militants killed many people: Hindus, Sikhs who opposed them, police, bus passengers.
In 1985 a bomb on an Air India flight from Canada killed three hundred twenty-nine people; a Canadian inquiry blamed militants based in Canada, though only one man was ever convicted.
The state's response was harsh too: young Sikh men were detained, and many disappeared.

A Sikh human rights worker named Jaswant Singh Khalra went through cremation records in Amritsar and found thousands of bodies burned as unidentified. In 1995 he was taken from outside his home and killed.
Police officers were later convicted. So the wait belongs to many: widows in Delhi, mothers in Punjab still asking where a son went, families who lost someone to a militant's gun.
Sikh teaching speaks of the Guru's justice, and of standing for the oppressed.
Justice delayed still matters. A verdict after thirty years can't give anyone back. But it says out loud that a wrong was a wrong, and that the names count.

how: Sikh organizations and families of 1984 survivors continue to press for justice through the courts, and each November gatherings remember the dead and the widows who waited.

o: justice, a wrong named as wrong

games.q: you're Jaswant Singh Khalra in Amritsar in the 1990s. cremation records show thousands of bodies burned as unidentified. what do you do?
o: make the records public and ask for justice.
games.why: Khalra made the records public. in 1995 he was taken from outside his home and killed; police officers were later convicted.

practice: Think of anyone, anywhere, still waiting for justice: a family asking for answers, a case that's stuck, a community whose wrong was never named.
If you pray, hold them in your prayer; if you don't, keep them in mind and wish them strength for the waiting. If anger comes, let it be there without feeding it, and return to the breath.

wordCard.voice: Insaaf. Justice — the word on banners as survivors of 1984, many of them widows, waited decades for it, while violence reached Punjabi families of every background.

orig.note: Punjabi (from Persian): insaaf, justice; the word on many banners at 1984 remembrances.

carryVoice: Your line: justice delayed still matters. For some, the wait isn't over. That's day three hundred eleven.

sources.ref: Justice Nanavati Commission Report, 2005, and earlier commissions on November 1984
